NO. 001 · Songbirds & City Birds / Hirundinidae · Swallows

Barn Swallow

家燕 · jiā yàn Hirundo rustica
Summer visitor Abundant 15–19 cm Protected (China) IUCN LC

The bird that builds its nest under your eaves

Steel-blue back, chestnut throat, deeply forked tail — in flight it looks like a pair of scissors. Barn Swallows live almost entirely alongside people: their mud cups go under eaves, on beams and inside bridge arches, and generation after generation comes back to the same spot.

Gallery

One scientific illustration for shape and colour blocks, two field photographs for how it looks in real light. Click any image to enlarge.

Identification

  • HeadForehead and throat chestnut; upperparts steel-blue with a metallic sheen; lores black.
  • UnderpartsA black breast band over a white to pale orange belly — the decisive difference from other swallows.
  • TailDeeply forked, the outer feathers drawn into long streamers with white spots at the tips; males average longer streamers than females.
  • FlightFast and agile, skimming low over ground or water, banking sharply with the wingtips almost closed.

Behaviour

Feeds on flying insects almost continuously, perching only to nest and rest. Builds a half-cup of mud pellets mixed with grass stems under eaves and beams, lined with feathers. A summer visitor in South China, arriving in March and leaving in October, with a few birds overwintering locally. Roosts communally in reedbeds or on wires.

Where to find it in Zhuhai

  • Doumen village eaves
  • Tangjiawan Old Town
  • skies over Jinwan farmland
  • old dwellings across the districts
Field note
Telling swallows apart: Barn Swallow has a black breast band and a deep fork. Red-rumped Swallow has an orange-red rump and a shallower fork. A mud nest under an eave is almost always this species.
